followUps:
In a domain-agnostic shared/data-access library, or better in an auth domain's data-access, exposed through its public index.ts. Almost every feature needs the user, so it is a legitimate cross-cutting dependency.

Keep it small: a signal user(), isLoggedIn() and roles. Do not put profile editing there; that belongs to the account domain. Providing it with providedIn: 'root' keeps one instance for the whole app.

By giving it strict rules: only code that at least two domains really use, and nothing with business logic. Everything else moves back into the domain that owns it.

Enforce it: shared is split into typed libraries (shared-ui, shared-util), each with a CODEOWNERS entry and a review rule that a new shared item needs two consuming teams. A thing used by one team stays in that team's library. Duplicating three lines is cheaper than a wrong shared abstraction.

Only when something must be built, deployed or scaled on its own: a separate audience (admin vs public site), a different release cadence, or different hosting such as SSR for marketing pages.

Until then one app with lazy routes into feature libraries is simpler, since libraries already give code isolation. Several apps in the same Nx workspace still share libraries, so the split costs little, but each app adds a pipeline to maintain.

It can be, as long as the state is only about how it looks. Open/closed, the month being viewed or a focused day are UI state and may live inside it.

It stops being presentational if it fetches holidays or writes to a store. The rule: the picked value comes in via input() or a model, and changes go out via output(). Internal state is fine; data fetching and app state are not.

Instantiate the class or use a light render helper, set inputs, and assert on outputs and the rendered result. Signal inputs can be set with fixture.componentRef.setInput, but pure logic can be tested with no TestBed at all.

Keep calculations in plain functions: pageCount(95, 10) === 10 needs no Angular. Use TestBed only for template checks such as DOM text and emitted events, because it is the slowest part.

It makes tests simpler, because a component test fakes one small object instead of a whole store.

In the test you provide { provide: FlightsFacade, useValue: { flights: signal([f1]), loading: signal(false), search: jasmine.createSpy() } }. No actions, selectors or HTTP mocks. The facade itself is tested once against the real store or an HTTP testing backend. Result: UI tests check rendering and calls, state tests check logic.

Signals for state the template reads, such as flights, loading and error. Templates and computed work with them directly and there is no subscription to manage.

Use Observables only for event streams, such as a search results stream you want to debounce or cancel. If a consumer needs RxJS it can use toObservable(). Mixing both in one facade confuses callers, so choose signals as the default.

code.title: Module-boundary check with tags

followUps:
Start in report-only mode, then fix by priority. Do not turn on all the rules at once; the build would fail with hundreds of errors.

  1. Add tags to every project and write the constraints.
  2. Run the lint rule as a warning and count violations per rule.
  3. Block new violations first (a ratchet), then fix the old ones team by team.
  4. Use temporary eslint-disable with a ticket for the hard ones.

Circular dependencies come first, since they block everything else.

Make the dependency explicit instead of bypassing the rule: expose a small contract through a shared library or the other domain's public API.

Example: checkin needs the booking reference type. Put BookingRef in a shared-types library tagged scope:shared, which both may import. If checkin needs behaviour, call it through an interface or an event, not by importing booking internals. Add a narrow exception to the constraints only after the owners agree.

When two parts need to be released independently and the organisation cannot coordinate their release train: different vendors or companies, very different cadences, or a legacy app being replaced piece by piece.

Wanting faster builds is not enough, as Nx caching and affected builds fix that. Code ownership is not enough either; CODEOWNERS and tags fix that. Split only when the cost of waiting for another team's release is higher than running extra pipelines and shared-dependency rules.

Put them in the host as shared singletons, and let remotes read them from there. The remote never re-implements login, it just uses the shared service.

With Native Federation you list auth and design-system libraries in the shared config with singleton: true, so one instance exists on the page. Design tokens as CSS custom properties on :root pass through the page for free. Version the design system with semver and a strict range, so a remote cannot silently load an incompatible one.

First try to upgrade it, because a mismatch costs the most when it lives long. Federation tolerates one major difference only if you give up the shared singleton.

Options: the old remote brings its own Angular and is mounted as a Web Component or inside an iframe, which costs extra download and isolated change detection; or you set a deadline and upgrade it in the next release. Use a manifest with a version check and contract tests, so that the host knows which remote is lagging.

Because initFederation must set up the import map before any Angular code is imported. Static imports are evaluated first, so they would load Angular before the map exists.

main.ts is only initFederation(manifest).then(() => import('./bootstrap')). All real imports sit in bootstrap.ts, which runs after the map is set. Without this split, @angular/core would resolve normally and the host and remote could each load their own copy.

Treat exposed modules as a public API: a small, typed surface (for example only the route array) that you version and test from the consumer side.

Publish the contract as a TypeScript type in a shared library, and run contract tests in the host's CI that load each remote's built remoteEntry.json and check the exposed names. Add a version field to the manifest, keep changes additive, and deprecate before removing. A breaking change means a new exposed name such as ./routes-v2.

Define every colour as a design token (CSS custom property), and override the set under a theme selector. Components then read tokens only, so they need no change.

:root { --bg: #fff; --fg: #111; }
[data-theme='dark'] { --bg: #121212; --fg: #eee; }

Also respect prefers-color-scheme as the default, store the user's choice, and check contrast in both themes (4.5:1 for text). In Material 3 the same is done with color-scheme and light-dark() system tokens.

Make the shared component the easiest path, and the fork the harder one. People fork when the library is slow to change or too rigid.

Give a contribution path with a short review time, offer extension points (content projection, tokens, variants), publish a changelog, and track usage so you see who copied a component. Lint rules can flag imports of raw Material where a company wrapper exists. A design-system office hour helps more than a policy document.

A harness is a small test API for a component, so tests say await button.click() instead of querying CSS selectors. When the internal markup changes, only the harness changes, not every test.

Angular Material and CDK ship harnesses such as MatButtonHarness. For your own components you extend ComponentHarness with methods like getText() or selectOption(). They work in unit tests and in end-to-end runs, and they wait for async work automatically.

Use the locale-aware APIs, not string formatting. In Angular the date and currency pipes use the active locale, and underneath it is Intl.

Example: 1234.5 EUR is 1,234.50 € in en-US style but 1.234,50 € in de-DE. Store dates as UTC ISO strings and format only at display, with the user's time zone. Never hard-code a currency symbol or a date pattern; for built-in i18n, register locale data with registerLocaleData.

Layout, direction-based CSS and icons break. Text must flow right-to-left, and anything built with left/right ends up mirrored wrongly.

Fixes: set dir="rtl" on the root, use logical properties (margin-inline-start, padding-inline-end, inset-inline) instead of left/right, and flip directional icons such as arrows and back buttons. Numbers, phone numbers and code stay left-to-right. CDK Directionality tells components the current direction, and sliders and carousels need checking.

code.title: Escaping and sanitizing sinks

followUps:
Because a href can be cleaned: the dangerous part is the scheme, so javascript: is turned into unsafe: and the rest stays a normal link. A script or iframe src is different, since any URL loads and runs code from that origin, so no cleaning can make it safe.

That is why resource URLs throw unless you explicitly trust a value with bypassSecurityTrustResourceUrl, and you should do that only for constants or an allowlist of origins.

Trusted Types is a browser feature that makes dangerous DOM sinks (innerHTML, script.src) accept only special typed objects, not plain strings. A forgotten raw write then fails instead of running.

Angular can create these objects in its sanitizer, so framework code keeps working, while third-party or hand-written innerHTML = userText is blocked. You enable it with the CSP header require-trusted-types-for 'script' and name allowed policies. It is defence in depth, not a replacement for sanitizing.

code.title: XSRF cookie-to-header check

followUps:
Because GET requests should not change anything, so a forged GET cannot do harm, and adding the header to every read would be extra work with no gain.

The protection applies to mutating methods (POST, PUT, DELETE, PATCH). The rule only holds if your server really keeps GET read-only: an endpoint like GET /delete?id=5 breaks the model and stays open to CSRF. Fix the endpoint, not the interceptor.

The Angular interceptor skips absolute URLs, so you need your own scheme. The usual choice is a bearer token or a custom header that the browser does not add automatically.

Options: send Authorization: Bearer ... from an interceptor you write (CSRF is then not an issue, XSS becomes the risk); or fetch a CSRF token from the API (GET /csrf) and send it in a header with withCredentials. The API must also set a strict CORS allowlist, never * with credentials.

code.title: Filter, sort and paginate pipeline

followUps:
Make the URL the source of truth: read query params into signals, and write them back when the user changes something.

Use ActivatedRoute.queryParamMap with toSignal to read sort=age&dir=asc&page=2, and call router.navigate([], { queryParams, queryParamsHandling: 'merge' }) on change. Use replaceUrl: true for typing in the filter so history does not fill up. Reset page to 1 when sort or filter changes. Reload then reproduces the exact view.

With 1M rows you cannot send or render everything, so move work to the server and render only visible rows.

Server side: the API takes query, sort, page, size and returns one page plus a total count; use debounce and switchMap to cancel stale requests. Rendering: CDK virtual scroll keeps about 20 DOM rows regardless of size. Sorting 1M rows in the browser would block for a second or more, and you would still download the whole data set first.

Use real buttons inside the column header and tell assistive technology the current sort with aria-sort on the th.

<th scope="col" [attr.aria-sort]="dir()">
  <button (click)="sortBy('age')">Age</button>
</th>

Values are ascending, descending or none. The button gives keyboard and focus support for free. Announce result changes with a live region such as "12 results", and do not rely on an arrow icon alone to show the order.

They make Next wait, so the button should show a pending state and block double clicks until the check finishes. An async validator (for example a username check) leaves the control in PENDING.

Implementation: on Next, call markAllAsTouched(), then wait for group.statusChanges to leave PENDING (RxJS filter and take(1)) before checking valid. Use updateOn: 'blur' or a debounce in the validator to avoid a request on every key. Always handle a failed request as an error state.

Yes for a simple linear wizard, since it gives the step header, keyboard support and per-step validity cheaply. No when steps need their own URLs or complex branching.

MatStepper takes a [stepControl] per step and blocks Next when it is invalid with linear mode. It does not give browser Back support or route guards, and it keeps all step components in the DOM unless you use lazy content. For checkouts I prefer child routes and a route-scoped form service.

Signal Forms replace the reactive form object with a form model held in a signal, so values, validity and touched state are signals you can read in computed.

The wizard idea stays the same: one model for the whole flow, a sub-section per step, validation rules declared as schema functions, and a step signal. The gain is less boilerplate and no manual subscriptions to valueChanges. The API is still evolving, so check the current docs before relying on details.

code.title: Immutable kanban move with fractional rank

followUps:
Decide a rule, then make the loser see it. With plain last-write-wins, the second save silently overwrites the first, so it is best avoided.

Send a version number with each move; the server rejects a move based on an old version with 409 and returns the current board. The client rolls back, applies the new state and tells the user "Sam moved this card". Fractional ranks reduce conflicts, since two moves of different cards touch different rows. Real-time sync (WebSocket) makes conflicts rare.

Render only the cards in view, using cdk-virtual-scroll-viewport inside each column with a fixed itemSize. This keeps the DOM small when a column has thousands of cards.

Care is needed with drag and drop: the drop list index refers to the visible window, so convert it to a real index using the viewport's rendered range. Auto-scroll while dragging is limited. A common alternative is paging a column with "load more", which suits kanban better than infinite lists.
